paragraphs.heading: Pairs of inputs and outputs
paragraphs.text: The graph of a function f is the collection of all ordered pairs (x, y) where f(x) = y. In the everyday case, where both x and f(x) are real numbers, each pair gives the Cartesian coordinates of a point in a plane. Together those points often trace out a curve. A drawing of the graph is also called a plot.

paragraphs.heading: Two inputs make a surface
paragraphs.text: Some functions take a pair of numbers (x, y) as their input. For these the graph usually means the set of triples (x, y, z) where f(x, y) = z. Those triples sit in three-dimensional space. When the function is continuous, real-valued and takes two real inputs, the triples form a surface, which can be drawn as a surface plot.

paragraphs.heading: Adding guides to a picture
paragraphs.text: It often helps to draw the gradient of the function and several level curves along with it. The level curves can be drawn right on the surface or projected down onto the bottom plane. One such picture shows f(x, y) = −(cos (x²) + cos (y²))².

paragraphs.heading: Is a function just its graph
paragraphs.text: Every function's graph is one particular kind of relation. In the modern foundations of mathematics, usually set theory, a function actually is its graph. Strictly, though, a function is a triple: its domain, its codomain and its graph. People keep both words because each points to a different way of looking at the same object.

paragraphs.heading: What the graph leaves out
paragraphs.text: It is often useful to think of a function as a mapping, which records not only how inputs relate to outputs but also which set is the domain and which is the codomain. The graph alone does not settle the codomain. That matters for questions such as whether a function is onto, also called surjective, which depends on the codomain.

paragraphs.heading: Graphs at work
paragraphs.text: Science, engineering, technology, finance and many other fields use graphs as working tools. In the simplest case one quantity is plotted as a function of another, usually on rectangular axes.
